questions.q: Which pandas tool is the closest equivalent to SQL's CASE WHEN with two outcomes?
questions.explain: np.where evaluates a condition for every row and returns one value where True and another where False. np.select handles more than two outcomes.

questions.q: np.where(o["amount"] >= 100, "large", "small") is run on a row where amount is NaN. What label does that row get?
options: small, because NaN >= 100 evaluates to False
questions.explain: Comparisons with NaN are False, so the row silently falls into the else branch. Handle missing values explicitly when they matter.

questions.q: What happens to values that are not listed in the dictionary you pass to Series.map()?
options: They are deleted from the DataFrame
questions.explain: map replaces each value using the dictionary, and any value without a matching key becomes NaN.

questions.q: You call df.rename(columns={"amount": "total"}) and then print df. What do you see?
options: df with the column renamed, because rename always modifies in place
An error, because rename does not exist
df unchanged, because rename returned a new DataFrame that was not assigned
questions.explain: rename and drop return a new DataFrame. Assign the result back (df = df.rename(...)) to keep the change.

questions.q: Which is generally preferred when you can express the same result either way?
options: Vectorized operations such as arithmetic, np.where or map, rather than apply with a lambda
apply with a lambda, because it is always faster
A Python for loop over every row
Converting the column to text first
questions.explain: Vectorized operations are faster and easier to read. Reserve apply for logic that has no vectorized equivalent.
